drills.q: Rewrite `@dec\ndef f(): ...` without decorator syntax, and state precisely when the rewritten assignment happens.
drills.a: def f(): ...\nf = dec(f) — this runs once, at definition (module import) time, not on each call to f.

drills.q: You decorate a function without functools.wraps. What does `decorated_func.__name__` print, and name one framework-level consequence beyond cosmetics.
drills.a: It prints 'wrapper' (or whatever the inner function was named), not the original name. Consequence: frameworks that introspect the signature via inspect.signature (e.g. FastAPI's dependency injection) see (*args, **kwargs) instead of the real parameters and can break.

drills.q: Expand `@retry(times=3)` above `def call(): ...` into the equivalent explicit assignment, naming what each nested function layer is responsible for.
drills.a: call = retry(times=3)(call). Layer 1 (retry) takes the decorator's own arguments and returns the real decorator. Layer 2 (the returned decorator) takes the function and returns the wrapper. Layer 3 (wrapper) is what actually replaces calls to call.

drills.q: Given `@a` above `@b` above `def f(): ...`, write the equivalent assignment, then state which wrapper's code executes first when f() is called.
drills.a: f = a(b(f)). At call time execution is outside-in: a's wrapper code runs first (it's now the outermost callable), which then calls into b's wrapper, which finally calls the original f.

drills.q: A class has `@lru_cache(maxsize=None)` directly on an instance method `predict(self, x)`. Explain precisely why instances of this class never get garbage collected.
drills.a: The cache is attached to the function object shared across the class, and the cache keys include self as part of the argument tuple. Every instance that has ever called predict() is therefore referenced by the cache for the process's lifetime, so its refcount never reaches zero and it can't be collected.

drills.q: What's the correct fix for the lru_cache-on-instance-method leak if you need a cached value computed once per instance?
drills.a: functools.cached_property — it stores the computed value directly in the instance's own __dict__ rather than in a class-level cache, so the cached value is collected along with the instance itself.

drills.q: Why does `@lru_cache` raise TypeError: unhashable type: 'list' when a function is called with a list argument, and why is this treated as a feature rather than worked around by hashing the list's contents?
drills.a: The cache builds its key by hashing the arguments, and list/dict/set are unhashable. It's deliberate: even if the contents were hashed, using a mutable object as a cache key is a correctness hazard, because mutating that same list object after the call wouldn't invalidate the now-stale cached result.

drills.q: You add functools.wraps to a decorator but a static type checker (mypy) still doesn't flag a caller passing wrong argument types to the decorated function. Why, and how do you fix it?
drills.a: functools.wraps only restores runtime metadata (__name__, __doc__, __wrapped__) — it does not change the wrapper function's own static type signature, which is still (*args: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> Any. Fix by typing the decorator with ParamSpec and TypeVar: def dec(func: Callable[P, R]) -> Callable[P, R], with wrapper typed as (*args: P.args, **kwargs: P.kwargs) -> R.

drills.q: Distinguish a class decorator from a class used as a decorator, and give a reason to prefer the latter.
drills.a: A class decorator is a function applied to a class (receives/returns a class object, e.g. a registration pattern). A class used as a decorator implements __call__ and wraps a function; prefer it when the decorator needs to hold non-trivial state or expose extra methods to callers (e.g. a call counter with a .reset() method), which is awkward to expose cleanly from a plain closure.

drills.q: A function that worked fine with multiprocessing.Pool suddenly fails to pickle after you added a decorator to it. functools.wraps is present. What are the two most likely root causes?
drills.a: (1) The wrapper function is defined as a local/nested function rather than at module scope — pickle resolves functions by reference (module + qualname), and a purely local function can't be looked up that way regardless of wraps. (2) The decorator's closure captures something unpicklable (a lock, file handle, or lambda) that gets serialized along with it. wraps fixes the __name__/__qualname__ metadata but doesn't make an inherently unpicklable closure picklable.

drills.q: Explain why `@app.route('/x')` above `@login_required` above `def handler(): ...` runs the routing framework's wrapper code before the auth check, and what would go wrong if you needed metrics wrapped around the entire request including auth.
drills.a: Build order is handler = app.route('/x')(login_required(handler)), so app.route's wrapper is outermost and runs first at call time, then calls into login_required's wrapper. A metrics decorator placed inside login_required (closer to handler) would only time the work after auth passed, missing time spent in the auth check itself — it needs to be placed outside login_required, closer to app.route, to capture the whole request.
